what_its_for: Acitretin is used to treat severe psoriasis (a skin condition that causes red, scaly patches) and other serious skin disorders. It belongs to a group of medicines called retinoids, which are related to vitamin A. It helps slow down the growth of skin cells that build up and cause scaly patches.
how_to_take: Take acitretin by mouth, exactly as your doctor tells you. Always take it with a main meal that contains some fat (like your lunch or dinner) because food helps your body absorb the medicine better. Swallow the capsule whole — do not crush or chew it. Take it at the same time every day to help you remember. Do not take more or less than your prescribed dose.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight, skin condition, and how well you respond to treatment. A typical starting dose is 25 to 50 mg once a day. Your doctor may adjust your dose over time. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still the same day. If it is the next day already, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store acitretin at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep it away from light, heat, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the bottle tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: ALCOHOL: Do not drink alcohol while taking acitretin AND for at least 2 months after you stop taking it. Alcohol can cause a dangerous interaction that keeps the medicine in your body much longer and can cause serious harm. PREGNANCY: This medicine causes severe birth defects. Women who can become pregnant must use TWO forms of birth control for 1 month before starting, during treatment, and for 3 years after stopping acitretin. Do not donate blood while taking this medicine or for 3 years after stopping. Avoid taking vitamin A supplements or other retinoid medicines (like isotretinoin or tretinoin) at the same time. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen, as this medicine can make your skin more sensitive to the sun. Avoid wax hair removal, skin procedures, or dermabrasion during treatment and for about 6 months after stopping, as this medicine affects skin healing.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: severe headache, nausea, vomiting, or vision changes (signs of increased pressure in the brain); chest pain or difficulty breathing; muscle or joint pain that is severe; yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or stomach pain (signs of liver problems); depression, mood changes, or thoughts of harming yourself; severe skin peeling, blistering, or a painful rash; very dry or cracked lips, dry eyes, or nosebleeds that are bothersome; numbness or tingling in your hands or feet; or if you think you might be pregnant.
when_it_works: Acitretin does not work right away. Most people start to see improvement in their skin after 2 to 4 weeks, but it may take up to 3 to 6 months to see the full benefit. Keep taking the medicine as directed, even if you do not see results right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: PREGNANCY: Acitretin must NEVER be used during pregnancy. It causes very serious birth defects. A special program called the Do Your P.A.R.T. program requires all patients to be enrolled before receiving this medicine. WOMEN OF CHILDBEARING AGE: You must have a negative pregnancy test before starting, use two reliable forms of birth control, and continue birth control for 3 years after stopping. BREASTFEEDING: Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. CHILDREN: This medicine is generally not recommended for children unless specifically prescribed by a specialist, as it may affect bone growth. OLDER ADULTS: Use with caution; your doctor may start you on a lower dose. LIVER OR KIDNEY PROBLEMS: Tell your doctor if you have any liver or kidney problems, as this may affect whether you can safely use this medicine.
